prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

COLOMBO, Sri Lanka (CNN) -- Five members of the Sri Lanka's Civil Defense Force (CDF) were killed in a suicide blast in Sri Lanka at a church outside the capital of Colombo Sunday morning, police said. Sri Lankan police officers investigate Sunday's suicide bombing near Colombo. Eight other CDF officers and two civilians were wounded, police said. Nobody immediately claimed responsibility for the blast, but police suspect the bomber was a member of the Tamil Tiger rebels. There was no immediate response from the Tamil Tiger rebels to the incident, which, police said, occurred at St. Anne's Church in the Colombo suburb of Wattala, located on a roadway to the country's only international airport about 15 kilometers (9 miles) north of the capital. The attack happened during a weekly festival that usually draws a large crowd shopping for vegetables and household goods. The suicide bomber walked into an area where CDF officers were stationed and detonated his explosives, police said. Investigators suspect the bomber targeted the area because 150 police officers who help patrol the road to the airport are billeted there. Government forces have engaged rebels in heavy fighting for more than a year in the Kilinochchi region, once the center of political power for the Tamil Tigers. The 25-year civil war between ethnic Tamil separatists and the Sri Lankan government has left more than 65,000 people dead. The Tamil Tigers were founded in 1976, and the U.S. State Department designated the group a foreign terrorist organization in 1997. The rebels, formally known as the Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam (LTTE), are fighting for the creation of an independent nation, citing discrimination by the country's Sinhalese majority. Earlier Sunday, Sri Lanka's navy said it had destroyed a Tamil Tiger rebel boat allegedly attempting to smuggle in military supplies through the northern coast. Commander D.K.P. Dissanayake, a navy spokesman, told CNN that four rebels were killed in attack after the boat was engulfed in fire. He said the incident occurred just after midnight Sunday but gave no other details. There was no immediate response from the Tiger rebels to that incident. CNN could not independently verify the government's claim because media is debarred from Sri Lanka's battle zones. In the past, both sides in the conflict have exaggerated accounts of military operations. On December 20, the Navy said it destroyed a similar rebel boat trying to smuggle military supplies through the coast near the northeastern coastal village of Mullaitivu. However, a second supply boat was caught on Air Force aerial surveillance cameras unloading along the coast. "They included assorted ammunition, artillery shells, mortar shells and other items," a senior Air Force official told CNN. He spoke on grounds of anonymity since he was not authorized to speak to the media.

Sri Lankan police were seen examining the scene of the bombing near Colombo. Authorities said eight additional CDF personnel and two civilians were injured in the attack.

No group immediately said it was behind the explosion, though police believe the attacker may have belonged to the Tamil Tiger rebels. The rebels did not immediately comment on the bombing.

According to police, the blast took place at St. Anne’s Church in Wattala, a suburb of Colombo situated on the road leading to Sri Lanka’s only international airport, roughly 15 kilometers, or 9 miles, north of the capital.

The bombing occurred during a weekly market festival that typically attracts many people buying vegetables and household items. Police said the attacker entered a section where Civil Defense Force officers were posted and then set off his explosives.

Investigators think the location may have been chosen because about 150 police officers assigned to patrol the airport road are housed there.

Sri Lankan government troops have been locked in intense battles with rebels for more than a year in the Kilinochchi area, which was formerly the Tamil Tigers’ political stronghold.

The civil conflict, now 25 years old, pits ethnic Tamil separatists against the Sri Lankan government and has killed more than 65,000 people.

The Tamil Tigers were established in 1976. In 1997, the U.S. State Department placed the organization on its list of foreign terrorist groups. Officially called the Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam, or LTTE, the rebels say they are fighting to establish a separate state, arguing that Tamils face discrimination from Sri Lanka’s Sinhalese majority.

Earlier the same Sunday, Sri Lanka’s navy said it had destroyed a Tamil Tiger vessel that it accused of trying to bring military supplies into the country through the northern coast.

The Tamil Tiger rebels also gave no immediate reaction to the navy’s account. CNN was unable to independently confirm the government’s statement because journalists are barred from Sri Lanka’s combat areas.

Both the government and the rebels have previously overstated their descriptions of military actions.

On December 20, the navy said it had destroyed another rebel boat allegedly attempting to move military supplies through waters near Mullaitivu, a village on the northeastern coast. But a second supply vessel was recorded by Air Force aerial surveillance unloading cargo along the shoreline.

**Suicide bombing at Sri Lankan church kills five security personnel**

**WATTALA, Sri Lanka** — A suicide bomber struck outside St. Anne’s Church in Wattala, north of Colombo, killing five members of Sri Lanka’s Civil Defense Force and injuring several others, authorities said.

The attacker detonated explosives near security personnel stationed at the church, officials said. The Civil Defense Force members were part of a local security presence guarding the area amid heightened concerns over attacks on civilian and religious sites.

Sri Lankan authorities said they suspected the involvement of the Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam, or LTTE, the separatist militant group commonly known as the Tamil Tigers. There was no immediate claim of responsibility.

Emergency crews and police rushed to the scene after the blast, while the injured were taken to nearby hospitals. Security forces sealed off the area and launched an investigation into how the attacker approached the church compound.

The bombing comes against the backdrop of Sri Lanka’s long-running civil war, which pitted government forces against the LTTE, a group seeking an independent Tamil homeland in the north and east of the island. The conflict, which began in 1983, has killed tens of thousands of people and displaced many more.

The Tamil Tigers have been accused of carrying out numerous suicide bombings and attacks on political, military and civilian targets during the war. The group has also denied responsibility for some attacks attributed to it by the government.

Wattala, located near the capital and home to a mixed community of Sinhalese, Tamils and Catholics, has been considered strategically sensitive because of its proximity to Colombo and key transport routes.

Authorities said additional security measures were being put in place at churches and public gathering sites following the attack.

**COLOMBO, Sri Lanka (CNN)** — A suicide bomber detonated explosives Sunday in the town of Wattala, north of Sri Lanka’s capital, killing and wounding members of the Civil Defence Force and civilians, authorities said.

Officials said the attacker struck near a group of CDF officers in the largely urban area just outside Colombo. Several civilians caught in the blast were among the casualties, according to police and hospital sources. The exact number of dead and injured was not immediately clear.

Sri Lankan authorities said they suspected the Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam, or LTTE, was responsible for the bombing. The rebel group, which has carried out suicide attacks in the past, did not immediately claim responsibility.

Security forces sealed off the area after the explosion and began searching for possible accomplices, officials said. Roads around the blast site were temporarily closed as investigators examined debris and collected evidence.

The attack comes amid Sri Lanka’s long-running conflict between government forces and the LTTE, a Tamil separatist group that has fought for an independent homeland for ethnic Tamils in the north and east of the island nation. The war, which began in the early 1980s, has killed tens of thousands of people and displaced many more.

The LTTE, also known as the Tamil Tigers, has been designated a terrorist organization by several countries. The group has been accused of using suicide bombers, political assassinations and attacks on military and civilian targets. The rebels say they are fighting discrimination against Sri Lanka’s Tamil minority by the Sinhalese-dominated government.

Sri Lanka’s government has vowed to defeat the rebels militarily, while human rights groups have repeatedly raised concerns about civilian casualties, disappearances and abuses by both sides.

Sunday’s bombing underscored fears that violence could continue to spread beyond the main battle zones in the north and east, striking heavily populated areas near the capital.

**Suicide bombing near church and naval clash signal sharp escalation in Sri Lanka’s civil war**

**COLOMBO, Sri Lanka** — Sri Lanka’s long-running civil war appeared to enter a more volatile phase after a suicide attack near St. Anne’s Church outside Colombo and a separate sea battle between the Sri Lankan navy and Tamil Tiger rebels off the island’s northern coast, incidents that underscored the widening reach of the conflict from contested northern waters to the capital’s outskirts.

Security officials said a suicide bomber struck near the Roman Catholic church in a suburb outside Colombo, an area that had been on heightened alert amid fears of renewed attacks by the Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam, or LTTE. The blast caused casualties and sent worshippers, residents and security personnel fleeing through streets littered with debris. Ambulances and police vehicles converged on the scene as authorities sealed off surrounding roads and began searching for possible accomplices.

There was no immediate independent confirmation of who carried out the attack, but Sri Lankan officials blamed the LTTE, which has a long history of suicide bombings against political, military and civilian targets. The Tigers, who have fought for decades to create an independent Tamil homeland in the north and east of the Sinhalese-majority island, have often denied responsibility for attacks that caused civilian casualties.

The bombing near St. Anne’s Church was particularly alarming because it struck close to a place of worship in the heavily populated western belt around Colombo, where the government has expanded checkpoints, roadblocks and intelligence operations in response to rebel attacks. Police said investigators were examining remains at the blast site and reviewing the movements of the suspected bomber before the explosion.

The attack came as Sri Lanka’s navy reported a confrontation with Tamil Tiger vessels off the northern coast, a region central to the rebels’ supply network and one of the most contested areas of the war. Naval officials said patrol craft engaged rebel boats in waters near the northern coastline, where the LTTE’s naval wing, known as the Sea Tigers, has previously staged ambushes, suicide boat attacks and arms-smuggling operations.

According to the military, the clash erupted when navy units intercepted suspected rebel craft operating in restricted waters. Officials said the navy opened fire after the boats failed to comply with orders, triggering a battle that lasted for a significant period and involved multiple vessels. The military claimed rebel boats were damaged or destroyed and said casualties were believed to have been inflicted on the Tigers. As in many engagements at sea, the claims could not be independently verified, and the LTTE has often issued sharply different accounts of such encounters.

The two incidents highlighted the dual nature of the conflict: a conventional military campaign in the north and east, and an insurgent-style campaign of bombings and assassinations in government-held territory. Analysts said the combination places pressure on the government, which has promised to crush the LTTE militarily, while also raising concerns about civilian security far from the front lines.

Sri Lanka’s civil war, rooted in ethnic tensions between the Sinhalese-dominated state and the Tamil minority, has killed tens of thousands of people since it erupted in the early 1980s. A Norwegian-brokered cease-fire signed in 2002 had largely collapsed after years of violations by both sides, and the government’s formal withdrawal from the truce marked the return to full-scale war. Since then, fighting has intensified across the north, with the army pushing into rebel-held territory and the navy trying to cut off maritime supply routes.

The LTTE once controlled large areas of the north and east and maintained its own police, courts and tax system in rebel-held zones. In recent years, however, government forces have recaptured key eastern territory and shifted focus to the Tigers’ northern strongholds, including the Vanni region. The rebels, under growing battlefield pressure, have increasingly relied on asymmetric tactics, including suicide attacks and strikes on civilian or symbolic targets.

The bombing near St. Anne’s Church drew condemnation from political and religious leaders, who warned that attacks near places of worship risk inflaming communal tensions in a country already scarred by decades of violence. Catholic clergy urged calm and called on authorities to protect civilians without resorting to arbitrary detentions or harassment of minority communities.

Human rights groups have repeatedly warned that the renewed war has been accompanied by disappearances, extrajudicial killings, child recruitment, restrictions on humanitarian access and attacks on civilians. Both the government and the LTTE have rejected many allegations, accusing each other of manipulating civilian suffering for political advantage.

In Colombo, the immediate response was a tightening of security. Police and soldiers increased checks on vehicles entering the capital, particularly vans, buses and motorcycles, which have been used in previous attacks. Commuters faced long delays as security forces inspected identity documents and searched bags. Authorities also warned the public to remain vigilant and report unattended parcels or suspicious activity.

The naval clash, meanwhile, reinforced the strategic importance of the waters around northern Sri Lanka. The LTTE’s ability to move fighters, weapons and supplies by sea has long been a central concern for the government. The navy has claimed a series of successes against rebel logistics vessels in recent years, while the Tigers’ Sea Tiger units have demonstrated an ability to strike coastal bases and naval patrols despite the government’s superior firepower.

Diplomats in Colombo said the latest violence could further narrow prospects for negotiations. International mediators have urged both sides to return to talks, but neither has shown willingness to compromise while battlefield momentum remains in question. The government insists the LTTE must be defeated militarily before any political settlement can be meaningful, while Tamil representatives argue that no lasting peace is possible without addressing minority grievances over power-sharing, language rights, security and regional autonomy.

For civilians, the escalation has deepened a sense of uncertainty. In the north, thousands remain displaced by fighting, shelling and shortages of food and medicine. Around Colombo, residents accustomed to periodic attacks said the bombing near a church was a reminder that even areas far from the front remain vulnerable.

As investigators continued work at the blast site and naval units maintained patrols off the northern coast, Sri Lanka faced the prospect of still more violence: a tightening battlefield in rebel-held areas, a determined military campaign by the state, and a rebel movement with a proven capacity to strike far beyond the war zone.
